title: Void Ending in a Trine to Uranus
source: Picatrix (adapted), Book I chapter 5, Book II chapter 3 and Book III chapter 1

<!-- generated by tools/content/gen-void.ts; edit the generator, not this file -->

The trine is the best of the aspects, the one the doctrine uses to tie the Moon to the fortunes. The text grades it as perfect friendship, because the signs it joins are of one element and gaze at each other in full agreement; works meant to endure are founded with the Moon fixed, and the lord of her house regarding her in trine or sextile.

When the Moon closes her course in a sign with a trine to Uranus, the quiet stretch that follows carries something of his cold, sky-borne surprises. Uranus is nowhere in Picatrix: the planet was found with a telescope in 1781, some seven centuries after the book was written, and no passage of the source speaks of it. What follows is this almanac's extension of Picatrix's doctrine, never the medieval text's own words. Named for the Greek god of the sky, it is read here as a cold, far, sky-colored planet of upheaval, so that a course closing on it ends on a surprise rather than a settled end.
